record_type_quote:
We tested the computational reproducibility of a research claim from Michal and Shah

(2024) according to which individuals assume that a scientific finding described in a media

report is meaningfully large when numerical information about the magnitude of this finding

is missing.

targets.title: A practical significance bias in laypeople’s evaluation of scientific findings.
targets.evidence_quote:
We tested the computational reproducibility of a research claim from Michal and Shah

(2024) according to which individuals assume that a scientific finding described in a media

report is meaningfully large when numerical information about the magnitude of this finding

is missing.
targets.outcome_computational_quote:
Using the dataset from the original study, we

successfully reproduced the focal test of the paper for both studies. We uncovered a

couple of errors in the process, which did not change the studies’ main results.
targets.outcome_robustness_quote:
We are happy to report that the reproduction was largely

successful in that we only found minor to moderate errors that do not challenge the

authors’ core conclusions. Altogether, the scope and implications of these errors do not

seem to necessitate a correction of the article.
targets.outcome_reasoning: The focal tests and ANOVA values were reproduced, with minor reported errors that the authors explicitly say do not change the conclusions. Both Tukey HSD and marginal-means calculations were actually tested and retain the central contrast conclusions; robustness is limited to these alternative calculations, not a broad sensitivity analysis.

reasoning: Primary complete reproduction report from the assigned OSF project matches title and all three authors. Reanalyses use original data for both original studies, aggregated as one target paper. The two calculation methods provide a limited tested robustness comparison, while most of the report addresses computation.
